197.title: The universal form (11.9–11.31)
197.hook: Arjuna gets what he asked for, and it's brighter than a thousand suns
197.howItsDone: The vishvarupa, the universal form of Gita chapter eleven, is painted, sculpted and staged across Hindu art and temple traditions, and many devotees read the chapter with awe as the Gita's great vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna asks to see, and gets a divine eye. Your line was show me. Today, he's shown. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Imagine the sky at noon, and the sun in it. Now imagine a second sun rising beside it. Then ten. Then a hundred. Then a thousand, all at once, all blazing. You can't look at it. You can't look away. In 1956 a book about the scientists who built the atomic bomb took its title from this chapter: Brighter than a Thousand Suns. The line it borrowed comes from the moment Arjuna, with his new divine eye, finally sees what he asked to see. Today, the vision itself.
screen: `ONE SUN AT NOON.` → `THEN A THOUSAND, AT ONCE.` → `BRIGHTER THAN A THOUSAND SUNS.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya, the narrator, tells it. Having spoken, the great lord of yoga showed Arjuna his supreme form. Many mouths and eyes, many wonders, divine ornaments, divine weapons raised. Faces turned in every direction. And verse twelve: if the light of a thousand suns were to blaze up in the sky all at once, it might be like the splendor of that great being. Verse thirteen: there, in the body of the god of gods, Arjuna saw the whole universe, divided in countless ways, gathered as one. His hair stands on end. He bows his head, joins his palms, and starts to speak. At first it's wonder. I see all the gods in your body, and all kinds of beings. Brahma on his lotus, the sages, the divine serpents. I see you everywhere, with countless arms and eyes. No end, no middle, no beginning. The sun and moon are your eyes. And then it turns. The mouths have fangs. The worlds are trembling, and so am I. And Arjuna sees the warriors of both armies, the men he's about to fight, his own teachers and great-uncle among them, rushing into those mouths, like rivers running into the ocean, like moths flying into a flame. Some are caught between the teeth. It's beautiful and it's terrifying, and the Gita doesn't soften either. Verse thirty-one: tell me, who are you, in this fierce form? I bow to you. Be gracious. I want to understand you; I don't know what you're doing. That's the word today, the universal form: everything, seen at once, including the parts that frighten us.
screen: `FACES IN EVERY DIRECTION.` · `THE LIGHT OF A THOUSAND SUNS.` · `NO END, NO MIDDLE, NO BEGINNING.` · `LIKE MOTHS INTO A FLAME.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: Sit, and start small: feel your own body, breathing. Then widen. Picture the room, the building, the street. Keep widening: the city, the whole country at this hour, people waking and sleeping, being born and dying. Then the earth, turning in sunlight. Let it be too big to hold. Notice what that feels like: wonder, fear, both. Then come back to one breath. The bell holds the time.
The universal form. Vishvarupa: the whole universe seen at once in God's body, brighter than a thousand suns, wonderful and terrible.
Your line: a thousand suns. Step outside once today, look near the sun without looking at it, and imagine a thousand. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: "I am Time" (11.32–11.34)
198.hook: the line Oppenheimer remembered, and what the Sanskrit word actually says
198.howItsDone: Hindus read Gita 11.32–34 in different ways: many as a warrior's duty and the power of time over every life, others, following Gandhi, as an allegory of the inner battle; the image of Kala, time, is also central in the worship of Shiva and Kali.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the universal form, brighter than a thousand suns, and Arjuna asking, who are you? Your line was a thousand suns. Today, the answer. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

July 1945, the New Mexico desert, before dawn. The first atomic bomb is tested, and a light brighter than anything anyone there has ever seen fills the sky. Twenty years later, in a television documentary, J. Robert Oppenheimer, who led the scientists who built it, remembered what went through his mind. He had studied Sanskrit, and read the Gita in the original. He recalled a line, in his own words: now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds. It's one of the most quoted sentences of the twentieth century. Today, the verse it came from, and what it actually says.
screen: `NEW MEXICO, 1945.` → `A LIGHT BRIGHTER THAN ANY BEFORE.` → `A LINE FROM THE GITA.`

segments.voice: Verse thirty-two begins: kalo 'smi. I am kala. Kala means time. It can also carry the sense of death, the way time eventually brings everything to an end, which is how Oppenheimer rendered it. Most translations say time. I am time, grown mighty, destroyer of worlds, here to bring the worlds to their end. Then the line that hits Arjuna hardest. Even without you, none of these warriors lined up in the opposing ranks will survive. Arjuna has spent eleven chapters agonizing over killing his teachers and his great-uncle. Krishna's answer is that time has already claimed them. Verse thirty-three: so stand up, win glory. They've already been struck down by me. You be only the instrument. Nimitta-matram: merely the occasion, the tool. Verse thirty-four names them: Drona, Bhishma, Karna, and the rest, already slain. Don't be distressed. Fight. This is one of the hardest passages in the Gita, and readers have taken it in very different ways. Many read it as it stands: a warrior's duty in a just war, and the truth that no one controls who lives and who dies. Mahatma Gandhi, who read the Gita every day, read the whole battlefield as an allegory of the war inside each person, and he took the Gita as a teaching of nonviolence. Either way, the verse says something everyone meets eventually: time is bigger than any of us, and we're asked to do our part without pretending we're in charge of the ending. That's today's word: I am Time.
screen: `KALA: TIME, AND ALSO DEATH.` · `EVEN WITHOUT YOU, NONE WILL SURVIVE.` · `BE ONLY THE INSTRUMENT.` · `A REAL WAR, OR THE WAR WITHIN.` · then, large: `I AM TIME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and listen for time. Maybe a clock ticking, your heartbeat, the breath coming and going. Each breath arrives and leaves; none of them stays. Let that be okay. Then think of one thing you're trying to control the ending of. Just for this sit, set the ending down. Your part is the next breath, and the next. The bell holds the time.
I am Time. Gita eleven, thirty-two: kala, time, which brings everything to its end. Oppenheimer rendered it as death.
Your line: time. Today, when you're gripping the outcome of something, remember: your part is the doing, not the ending. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: Arjuna's terror and praise (11.35–11.46)
199.hook: Arjuna realizes his best friend is God, and remembers every joke he ever made
199.howItsDone: Arjuna's hymn of praise in Gita 11.36–46 is recited by many Hindus in worship, and his plea for forgiveness shapes a common prayer habit of asking pardon for any disrespect shown in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday: I am Time, and be only the instrument. Your line was time. Did you set down one ending that isn't yours to control? Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Think of your oldest friend. The one you've known forever. You've teased them, beaten them at cards, shared a bed on a camping trip, eaten off their plate without asking, called them ridiculous nicknames. Now imagine that one day you find out who they really are, and it's bigger than anything you ever imagined. Your first thought might not be wow. It might be: oh no. All those jokes. All those times I treated you like just anybody. That is exactly where Arjuna finds himself, trembling, palms pressed together, in today's verses.
screen: `YOUR OLDEST FRIEND.` → `THE TEASING, THE NICKNAMES.` → `OH NO. ALL THOSE JOKES.`

segments.voice: Sanjaya says Arjuna, trembling, bows and speaks with a choked voice. First, praise. It's right that the world rejoices in you and loves you, Arjuna says. The frightened spirits flee in every direction, and the perfected ones bow. Why wouldn't they? You are the first god, the ancient person, the final resting place of the universe. You are the wind, death, fire, the lord of waters, the moon, the father of all creatures, and the great-grandfather. And then a line that sounds like someone who doesn't know where to put himself. Bowing to you a thousand times, and again, and again. Bowing in front, bowing behind, bowing on every side. And then the confession. Verses forty-one and forty-two. Thinking you were just my friend, I called you rashly: hey Krishna, hey Yadava, hey friend. I didn't know how great you were. Out of carelessness, or out of love, whatever disrespect I showed you as a joke, while playing, resting, sitting or eating, alone or in front of others, I ask you to forgive it, immeasurable one. Verse forty-four: bear with me as a father with a son, a friend with a friend, a lover with the beloved. Notice what he asks for. Not to be distant. Not to go back to formality. He asks for the relationship to hold. And verse forty-five: I'm thrilled to have seen what no one has seen, and my mind is shaking with fear. Please, show me the form I know. That's today's word: Arjuna's terror and praise. Both at once.
screen: `TREMBLING, HE BOWS.` · `A THOUSAND TIMES, ON EVERY SIDE.` · `HEY KRISHNA, HEY FRIEND.` · `AS A FRIEND WITH A FRIEND.` · then, large: `FORGIVE MY FAMILIARITY.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of someone you've taken for granted. A parent, a partner, a friend who's always there. Picture them the way Arjuna finally saw Krishna: bigger, more precious than you usually let yourself notice. Let a little awe come in. Then, silently, say to them what Arjuna said: forgive me for treating you like just anybody. And, like Arjuna, ask for the closeness to stay. The bell holds the time.
Arjuna's terror and praise. Seeing his friend as God, he bows a thousand times, and asks forgiveness for every careless word.
Your line: forgive my familiarity. Today, tell one person you've taken for granted that you see them. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: The gentle form returns (11.47–11.55)
200.hook: after the thousand suns, the friend's face comes back, and Arjuna can breathe again
200.howItsDone: Most Hindu worship is directed to God in a gentle, familiar form, an image of Krishna, Rama, Shiva or the Goddess, and many devotees cite Gita 11.54–55 to say that loving devotion, not ritual alone, is how God is truly known.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna's terror and praise, and a friend asking to be forgiven for every joke. Your line was forgive my familiarity. Day two hundred. Two hundred days on this path. And today, the end of chapter eleven.
screen: `ARJUNA'S TERROR AND PRAISE — FORGIVE MY FAMILIARITY.`

segments.voice: Think of a child who's had a nightmare, shaking in the dark. The parent comes in and turns on the small lamp by the bed. Same room. Same shadows in the corners. But now there's a familiar face, and a voice that says, it's okay, I'm here. The child can breathe again. Arjuna has seen the whole universe blazing in Krishna's body, mouths and fire and time itself. And he asked, please, show me the form I know. Today, Krishna does.
screen: `A NIGHTMARE IN THE DARK.` → `A SMALL LAMP, A FAMILIAR FACE.` → `SHOW ME THE FORM I KNOW.`

segments.voice: Verse forty-seven: out of grace, through my own power, I showed you this highest form, full of light, universal, infinite, first. No one but you has seen it before. Verse forty-eight: not by the Vedas, not by sacrifice, not by study, not by gifts, not by rituals, not by fierce austerities can I be seen in this form by anyone but you. Then verse forty-nine, the tender turn. Don't be afraid. Don't be bewildered by seeing this terrible form of mine. Let your fear go, be glad at heart, and see my familiar form again. Sanjaya tells what happens. Krishna shows his own form again, and, becoming gentle in form, saumya, the great soul comforts the frightened Arjuna. Saumya is a lovely word: gentle, mild, moon-like, cool after heat. Arjuna, verse fifty-one: seeing this gentle human form of yours, I'm myself again. I've come back to my nature. And then Krishna says what the whole chapter was pointing at. This form you've seen is very hard to see; even the gods long to see it. Not by Vedas, not by austerity, not by gifts or sacrifice. But by devotion alone, bhakti, undivided, can I be known like this, seen truly, and entered. And the last verse of the chapter, which some call the essence of the whole Gita: whoever works for me, holds me as the goal, is devoted to me, free of attachment, and without hatred toward any being, comes to me. Without hatred toward any being. That's today's word, the gentle form returns. After the thousand suns, the friend's face, and the way to it: by devotion alone.
screen: `NO ONE BUT YOU HAS SEEN IT.` · `DON'T BE AFRAID.` · `SAUMYA: GENTLE, MOON-LIKE.` · `WITHOUT HATRED TOWARD ANY BEING.` · then, large: `BY DEVOTION ALONE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let yourself come down after a big week of chapters. Breathe out slowly, as if after a fright. Picture a familiar, gentle face, of God if you pray, or of someone who has comforted you. Let their presence say what Krishna said: don't be afraid. Let your shoulders drop. Stay with the gentleness, cool and quiet, like moonlight. The bell holds the time.
The gentle form returns. After the vision, Krishna takes his familiar human form again, and says he's truly seen by devotion alone.
Your line: by devotion alone. Today, be the gentle face for someone who's frightened or overwhelmed. Say, it's okay, I'm here. Day two hundred.

201.title: Form or formless? (12.1–12.7)
201.hook: love God with a face, or seek the reality beyond all faces? Arjuna asks which is better
201.howItsDone: Hindus worship God both with form (saguna), through images, names and stories, and as formless (nirguna), through silent meditation; many practice both, and chapter twelve is often read to honor each.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the gentle form returns, and God known by devotion alone. Your line was by devotion alone. Were you the gentle face for someone? Today, chapter twelve, the chapter of devotion. Day two hundred one.
screen: `THE GENTLE FORM RETURNS — BY DEVOTION ALONE.`

segments.voice: Walk into a Hindu home and you might find a shrine with a small image of Krishna, dressed in real clothes, offered food, put to bed at night. Walk into another and you might find a person sitting in silence, eyes closed, who'll tell you that God has no form at all, beyond every image and every name. Both are Hindu. Both are ancient. And people have argued for centuries about which comes closer. Arjuna has just seen God in the most overwhelming form imaginable, and then in a gentle human one. So chapter twelve opens with the obvious next question.
screen: `A SMALL IMAGE, DRESSED AND FED.` → `SILENCE, BEYOND EVERY FORM.` → `WHICH COMES CLOSER?`

segments.voice: Verse one, Arjuna: there are those who are always devoted to you, worshiping you. And there are those who worship the imperishable, the unmanifest. Which of these knows yoga best? Verse two, Krishna: those who fix their minds on me, always devoted, with the highest faith, I consider the most united. But then verses three and four: those who worship the imperishable, which can't be described, the unmanifest, present everywhere, beyond thought, unchanging, unmoving, firm, holding the senses in check, even-minded everywhere, delighting in the good of all beings, they also reach me. Both arrive. Then verse five names the difference: the difficulty is greater for those whose minds are set on the unmanifest, because the unmanifest path is hard for embodied beings. We have bodies. We love faces. And verses six and seven: those who offer all their actions to me, and meditate on me with undivided devotion, I quickly lift them out of the ocean of death and rebirth. Hindu teachers have read this passage very differently. In Advaita Vedanta, following Shankara, the formless is the final truth, and the path of form is the gentler road for most people. In devotional schools, following teachers like Ramanuja, devotion to the personal Lord is itself the highest, and they read verse two that way. What all of them find in the text is that both reach him, and that one is easier to walk. That's today's word: form or formless? Krishna's answer: either way.
screen: `WHICH KNOWS YOGA BEST?` · `THOSE DEVOTED TO ME: MOST UNITED.` · `THE FORMLESS PATH ALSO ARRIVES.` · `HARDER FOR THOSE WITH BODIES.` · then, large: `EITHER WAY.`

segments.voice: Try both, one minute each. First, form. Picture a face or an image that feels sacred to you: a deity, a teacher, a loved one, a candle flame. Hold it with warmth. Then, halfway through, let the image dissolve, and rest in what's left: silence, space, awareness without a shape. Notice which one feels closer today. There's no wrong answer; the Gita says both arrive. The bell holds the time.
Form or formless? Gita twelve: those devoted to God with a form, and those who seek the formless, both reach him. The formless is harder for embodied beings.
Your line: either way. Today, notice whether you reach for the sacred through something you can see, or through silence, and let both count. Day two hundred one.

202.title: The ladder of practice (12.8–12.12)
202.hook: Krishna gives a path with a step for every kind of day
202.howItsDone: Many Hindus read Gita 12.8–12.12 as permission to begin wherever they are: some meditate, some keep a daily practice like japa, and many simply offer their ordinary work and let go of the result.

segments.voice: Yesterday: form or formless? Arjuna asked which kind of devotee is best, the one who loves God with a face or the one who seeks the formless. Your line was either way. Both arrive. Today, what to do when neither feels possible. Day two hundred two.

Think of a good physical therapist. You come in after an injury and they say: today, walk to the door and back. You can't. Fine, they say. Stand up and sit down five times. You can't do that either. Fine. Squeeze this ball. Nobody leaves the room with nothing to do. There's always a smaller step that still counts. Chapter twelve of the Gita has a stretch that works exactly like that. Krishna has just said the goal. Then, instead of repeating it louder, he starts handing Arjuna smaller and smaller steps.
screen: `CAN'T WALK TO THE DOOR?` → `STAND UP AND SIT DOWN.` → `THERE'S ALWAYS A SMALLER STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the ladder, verses eight through eleven, told from the top. The highest rung: fix your mind on me, let your understanding rest in me, and you will live in me. That's the whole goal in one sentence. Then verse nine: if you can't hold your mind steady on me, then seek me through practice. The Sanskrit is abhyasa, practice, the repeating, coming back again and again. We met it in chapter six with the restless mind. Verse ten: if you can't even practice, then make your work for my sake. Do your ordinary actions as an offering, and you'll reach perfection that way. And verse eleven, the bottom rung: if you can't do even that, then take refuge in me, keep yourself in check, and give up the fruit of all your actions. Just let go of how it turns out. Four rungs, and each one begins with the same two words: if you can't. There's no scolding in it. No verse says if you can't, you've failed. Each one says, then here's the next thing. Then verse twelve turns the ladder around in a way that surprises people. Knowledge is better than practice, it says. Meditation is better than knowledge. And giving up the fruit of action is better than meditation, because peace follows that letting go right away. The lowest rung turns out to hold something the higher ones need. Commentators have argued about this verse for centuries, and they don't agree on exactly how to rank the steps. But they agree on the heart of it. Nobody is too busy, too scattered, or too far down to start. That's the word today: the ladder of practice.
screen: `FIX YOUR MIND ON ME.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, PRACTICE.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, WORK AS OFFERING.` · `IF YOU CAN'T, LET GO OF THE FRUIT.` · then, large: `THE LADDER OF PRACTICE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and try the top rung first. Rest your attention on whatever you hold most dear, a name, a face, or just stillness. When it slips, and it will, drop one rung. Come back to the breath, again and again. That's practice. If even that feels too much today, pick one thing you'll do after the bell and quietly dedicate it. And if you can't manage that, just let go of how today will turn out. Any rung counts. The bell holds the time.
The ladder of practice. Gita twelve, eight to twelve: fix your mind on the divine; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit.
Your line: if you can't, then… Today, when something good feels too big to do, don't quit it. Find the smaller rung and take that one instead. Day two hundred two.

203.title: The one dear to me (12.13–12.20)
203.hook: Krishna ends the chapter on devotion with a portrait, not a ritual
203.carry: free from hate, friendly to all
203.howItsDone: Many Hindus memorize or recite Gita chapter twelve, the chapter of bhakti, because it is short; its closing verses (12.13–12.20) are often read as a description of the devotee's character.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ladder of practice. Fix your mind; if you can't, practice; if you can't, work as offering; if you can't, let go of the fruit. Did you take a smaller rung? Day two hundred three.

You probably know one person like this. The friend who doesn't hold grudges. Who's the same at a wedding and a hospital. Who doesn't need you to agree with them. You leave their kitchen lighter than you came in, and you're never quite sure how they do it. Chapter twelve is the chapter of bhakti, devotion. You might expect it to end with instructions: which offering, which mantra, how many times. It doesn't. It ends with a portrait of a person. Eight verses, and a refrain that keeps coming back.
screen: `THE FRIEND WHO HOLDS NO GRUDGES.` → `NOT A RITUAL.` → `A PORTRAIT.`

segments.voice: Verse thirteen opens the portrait. The one who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free of mine and free of ego, the same in pleasure and pain, forgiving. In Sanskrit it starts adveshta sarva-bhutanam: without hatred toward all beings. Then maitra, friendly, a relative of the word for friend, and karuna, compassion. And each verse closes with some version of the same small phrase: sa me priyah. That one is dear to me. It's Krishna's voice, and it's tender. Verse fifteen is the one people repeat to each other. The one from whom the world does not shrink, and who does not shrink from the world. Nobody is afraid of them, and they aren't afraid of anybody. Then the portrait keeps going. Not elated, not hating, not grieving, not craving. The same to friend and enemy, in honor and in insult, in cold and in heat. Quiet. Content with whatever comes. And a surprising word in verse nineteen: aniketa, without a fixed home. Commentators read it as someone who doesn't cling to their house as the center of the universe, not necessarily someone homeless. Notice what isn't on the list. No rank. No caste. No particular ritual. The whole chapter on devotion ends by describing how a devoted person treats everyone else. Verse twenty closes the chapter: those who follow this with faith are exceedingly dear. That's the word today: the one dear to me. And that closes the chapter, and the week. We started with the vision that shook Arjuna, and we end with a kind face.
screen: `HATING NO BEING.` · `NO ONE AFRAID OF THEM.` · `THE SAME IN HONOR AND INSULT.` · `THAT ONE IS DEAR TO ME.` · then, large: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME.`

segments.voice: Sit, and bring to mind someone easy to love. Let yourself feel friendly toward them. Now someone neutral: a cashier, a neighbor you barely know. Offer them the same friendliness. Then, if you're willing, someone difficult. You don't have to fix anything. Just see if, for one breath, you can drop the hate and leave the friendliness. If that's too much today, go back to the easy one. The bell holds the time.
The one dear to me. Gita twelve, thirteen to twenty: a portrait of the devoted person, free of hate, friendly and kind, and the refrain, that one is dear to me.
screen: `THE ONE DEAR TO ME — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: free from hate, friendly to all. That's the week: the vision in chapter eleven, form or formless, the ladder, and the portrait. Today, let one person leave you lighter than they came. Day two hundred three.
